Getting started with zuxlsx

Source: vignettes/articles/zuxlsx.Rmd
zuxlsx.Rmd
library(zuxlsx)

zuxlsx reads .xlsx workbooks into R. It needs no system XML, ZIP or cryptography library: the parts it builds on are compiled into the package, so installing it is all there is to do. It reads; it does not write – see the end of this article for what to use instead.

The examples use a small workbook that comes with the package.

path <- system.file("extdata", "two-sheets.xlsx", package = "zuxlsx")

What is in the workbook

xlsx_sheets() lists the worksheets, in the order the workbook keeps them. It reads only the workbook’s index, not the sheets, so it costs the same on a small file as on a large one.

xlsx_sheets(path)
#> [1] "readings" "notes"

Reading a worksheet

xlsx_read() reads a worksheet into a data frame. By default it reads the first worksheet and takes the column names from its first row.

readings <- xlsx_read(path)
readings
#>   station reading checked      taken
#> 1   north   12.50    TRUE 2024-02-02
#> 2   south    9.75   FALSE 2024-02-03
#> 3    east   14.25    TRUE 2024-02-04

Each column takes the type its cells support. Nothing had to be declared: the numbers are doubles, the TRUE/FALSE cells are logical, and the dates – which an .xlsx stores as numbers with a date format – are Dates.

vapply(readings, function(x) class(x)[1], character(1))
#>     station     reading     checked       taken 
#> "character"   "numeric"   "logical"      "Date"

A column that mixes kinds of value, or holds a string or a cell error such as #DIV/0!, becomes character, with each cell as it was written. A date that carries a time of day becomes POSIXct rather than losing the time.

Choosing a worksheet, and part of one

sheet takes a name or a position.

xlsx_read(path, sheet = "notes")
#>                    note
#> 1 calibrated in January
#> 2                 µg/m³
identical(xlsx_read(path, sheet = 2), xlsx_read(path, sheet = "notes"))
#> [1] TRUE

range takes a rectangle in A1 notation. Either corner may name a cell, a column or a row, so "B1:C3", "A:B" and "2:4" all work.

xlsx_read(path, range = "B1:C3")
#>   reading checked
#> 1   12.50    TRUE
#> 2    9.75   FALSE

When the first row of what is read is data rather than names, say so with col_names = FALSE, and the columns are named by position.

xlsx_read(path, range = "A2:B4", col_names = FALSE)
#>      X1    X2
#> 1 north 12.50
#> 2 south  9.75
#> 3  east 14.25

Without range, the table is the rectangle the worksheet’s non-empty cells span, so one that starts further down the sheet, at B3 say, reads with its header from row 3.

When something is wrong

Every error zuxlsx raises carries a condition class, and the class – not the wording of the message – is what to rely on. A file that is not there is an input error; one that is not a ZIP archive at all is a ZIP error; a damaged part is an XML or ZIP error naming the part.

not_a_workbook <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
writeLines("this is not a spreadsheet", not_a_workbook)

tryCatch(
  xlsx_read(not_a_workbook),
  zuxlsx_zip_error = function(e) "not a readable xlsx file",
  zuxlsx_error = function(e) "some other problem"
)
#> [1] "not a readable xlsx file"

Every class is a subclass of zuxlsx_error, so one handler can catch them all. ?"zuxlsx-conditions" lists them. One is worth knowing early: a password-protected workbook read without a password is zuxlsx_encrypted_error, and every reader takes password = to open one.

When a data frame is the wrong shape

A worksheet is not always a table: a report with stacked blocks, a header several rows deep, notes in the margins. For those, xlsx_cells() returns one row per cell, with its position, its own type and its text, and xlsx_rows() returns the sheet row by row as text. xlsx_stream_cells() reads a sheet a chunk at a time, for one too large to hold, or to stop as soon as something is found.

head(xlsx_cells(path))
#>   row col   type   value number
#> 1   1   1 string station     NA
#> 2   1   2 string reading     NA
#> 3   1   3 string checked     NA
#> 4   1   4 string   taken     NA
#> 5   2   1 string   north     NA
#> 6   2   2 number    12.5   12.5

Writing workbooks

zuxlsx does not write .xlsx files, and is not going to. For that, use writexl for a plain data frame or openxlsx2 when formatting matters.
